projects.frameIsAnInteractiveProjectionInstallati: Frame is an interactive projection installation combining p5.js, web interaction, and an original animated story. It turns the abstract search for identity into a participatory experience, inviting visitors to recognize themselves beyond external judgments and define their own values and identity.
projects.deepInAForestStandsAMirror:
Deep in a forest stands a ‘Mirror of Truth.’ At night it projects people's shadows, surrounded by whispered sentences.
These words represent other people's judgments: sometimes blessings, sometimes pressure. As people become dependent on outside opinions, they lose touch with their own feelings.
A village legend says that anyone who finds the words ‘I am a person who…’ within their shadow can see themselves clearly and stop being defined by others.

The installation combines web interaction, an original animated story, p5.js, and the ml5.js BodyPix model. Participants' responses dynamically shape the visual output, turning the search for identity into a tangible experience of awareness and release from external expectations.

This was a group project. I handled p5.js body detection, technical integration, and experience-flow improvements.
projects.frameEncouragesPeopleToBreakFreeFrom:
Frame encourages people to break free from external judgments and redefine themselves.

Family expectations, social values, and mainstream culture can shape our self-image and distance us from our true feelings. The title refers both to these constraints and to a mirror that distorts our sense of self.

Participants search for their own statement among a sea of outside judgments. This makes the process of separating others' voices from one's inner voice visible and interactive. The work suggests that frames need not constrain our true selves; they can instead become opportunities for reflection and change, helping us build a more independent and authentic inner world.

projects.theP5JsExperienceHasFourStages:
The p5.js experience has four stages:
(1) Detect a visitor standing in front of the screen.
(2) Play the animation and instructions.
(3) Run the word-search game using silhouette detection.
(4) Play the appropriate ending.
The main technique uses ml5.js BodyPix for body segmentation. A point is considered inside the detected silhouette when its mask alpha is 0. This is used in stages one and three. During stage one, the silhouette is hidden and detection is used only to start the experience when someone arrives.
During the word-search stage, loadData() retrieves the website's answers and selects corresponding sentence arrays. These are shuffled and combined to generate background text. The participant's own sentence is inserted at a random position after it is received.
projects.theReactWebsiteIsBuiltIntoStatic:
The React website is built into static files with npm run build and served locally with Node.js and Express. Both exhibition computers share a network, allowing the other computer to access the site through the server's IP address and port. Answer selections and text are posted to the server, converted to JSON, and made available to p5.js.
The p5.js page refreshes for new data or after an experience ends, applying the next visitor's responses. Incoming data triggers an immediate refresh only during stage one, while the system is waiting for a visitor. This allows the questionnaire and the installation to serve two groups simultaneously without interrupting an active session, reducing waiting time.
projects.bothIntroductoryAnimationsOriginallyPlay: Both introductory animations originally played on the website, so visitors spent much longer outside the installation than inside it. projects.inspiredByCapsuleToyMachinesGotchaUses: Inspired by capsule-toy machines, GOTCHA uses generative randomness to create an ever-changing, playful universe. projects.gotchaTakesInspirationFromRowsOfCapsule:
GOTCHA takes inspiration from rows of capsule-toy machines and imagines them as a world of their own. Generative randomness echoes the surprise of turning a real machine. Randomly generated machines, backgrounds, and capsules change with each click, giving the work a playful, participatory quality.

Each capsule is built from many parameters: color, hair length and thickness, arrangement, and noise-driven direction changes that suggest organic growth. Around ten facial expressions correspond to the machines' designs. Capsule sizes, positions, and types also vary, from those inside the machine to those at its outlet or scattered outside. Some appear as transparent outlines; rare versions feature gradients.

Machines vary in color, shape, number, and position. Their faces and ears correspond to capsule features, giving the world a consistent visual language. Simple background shapes maintain a gentle style, and the background expands when only one machine appears to create a sense of space.

Clicking makes the capsules inside the central machine rotate and releases a new one. The previous capsule at the outlet is thrown into the surrounding scene. The result is a continuously growing, non-repeating landscape in which each interaction offers another surprise.
projects.flowFieldsSimulateUnderwaterAlgaeThrough: Flow fields simulate underwater algae through interweaving curves. Three layers—fine flowing lines, thicker complementary-color lines, and dots—add depth and texture. Each line is formed from circles whose direction follows noise-generated curvature, creating an organic sense of motion.
projects.thisWorkUsesFlowFieldsToEvoke:
This work uses flow fields to evoke underwater algae through interweaving, curved lines.

The canvas has three layers: fine lines generated from a noise field, thicker flow lines in complementary colors, and dots overlaid on the first layer for grain and depth. Curves consist of multiple circles with a color gradient from start to end. Each step changes direction according to noise, producing a natural flow.
projects.usingStackAndHillsTechniquesThisWork: Using Stack and Hills techniques, this work combines Perlin-noise curves, dark and murky colors, and hand imagery to evoke a river in the underworld. Lines grow like grass from stacked rectangles, bending with noise to suggest currents and wind.
projects.thisWorkUsesStackAndHillsTechniques:
This work uses Stack and Hills techniques, coordinate-based Perlin noise, dark and murky colors, and scattered hand imagery to evoke an underworld river.

A dense grid is scanned row by row. Noise offsets each position's height to form a rippling base. At each valid position, a blade of ‘grass’ is generated with noise- and randomness-driven length, thickness, and initial angle. Small rectangles stack step by step, changing direction with noise to suggest water or wind. Colors interpolate between two base tones, darker at the roots and lighter at the tips, while noise adjusts brightness to add fine grain.
projects.builtAroundRecursionAndBlocksThisWork: Built around Recursion and Blocks, this work repeatedly subdivides rectangles into a technological landscape resembling circuit boards and system interfaces. Pixel-like scan lines, varied borders, and shifts in color and opacity create a generative structure between digital interfaces and virtual space.
projects.usingRecursionAndBlocksThisWorkCreates:
Using Recursion and Blocks, this work creates a technological visual system from automatically divided rectangles and pixel-like lines.

A randomly selected main color establishes the background. ARect and BRect repeatedly divide the canvas horizontally or vertically at random ratios, producing a modular, circuit-board-like hierarchy. Large blocks are subdivided again; smaller ones are filled with different textures. ARect uses noise-controlled dotted lines to suggest scanning signals or pixel interference, while BRect uses borders of varying thickness to resemble interface boundaries or sensing areas. Random color offsets and opacity changes give the work the feel of a hologram or futuristic control panel. Recursion combines mechanical rules and randomness into a grid between code, circuitry, and virtual space.
projects.noiseAndColorControlGenerateAPlanet: Noise and color control generate a planet-like landscape of flowers and roots. Perlin noise shapes the flowers, while layers of dots gather into a spherical root system. Hue gradients and asynchronous drawing make the image emerge as if it were growing.
projects.thisWorkUsesNoiseAndColorControl:
This work uses noise and color control to create a planet-like landscape formed from flowers and roots.

The upper layer uses Perlin noise to determine flower height and tilt, creating natural-looking variation. Below, many noise-distributed dots extend downward and gradually collect into a sphere, like a planet made of roots. A random main color anchors the palette, while height controls hue gradients to contrast roots and petals. Step-by-step asynchronous drawing with await makes flowers appear one at a time, reinforcing the impression of life growing from noise.

projects.thisProjectGrewFromConcernAboutPeriod:
This project grew from concern about period poverty and stigma. Period poverty means lacking safe menstrual products, facilities, or education. It creates financial pressure for people on low incomes; the project report notes that around 9% of people in Taiwan have faced a choice between menstrual products and daily necessities. A lack of replacement products may bring health risks, while stigma frames menstruation as shameful or taboo and encourages people to hide products. Addressing these connected issues supports equity and human rights.
The nonprofit With Red had already created a Google-based map of period-friendly spaces offering free supplies, but it provided only locations and service categories. This project aims to offer a more practical, comprehensive website: sharing accurate information, reducing stigma, and improving the map with stock quantities and product specifications. The goal is to help people use these spaces confidently and support menstrual equity.

project_uiux_uiux1.thisRedesignOfExploreTaipeiNowFocuses: This redesign of Explore Taipei Now focuses on common trip-planning problems: insufficient information, inconvenient planning tools, and unintuitive interfaces.
project_uiux_uiux1.theOriginalAppLackedSufficientAttraction: The original app lacked sufficient attraction and transport information and complete itinerary tools, such as scheduling and travel options between stops. Its complex, repetitive structure offered little incentive to use it. Many travelers instead relied on Google Maps, but business-maintained information could be incomplete, and shortest-distance routes were not always the most convenient for sightseeing.
project_uiux_uiux1.theRedesignThereforeFocusesOnIntegrating: The redesign therefore focuses on integrating information, improving workflows, and making the app easier to use. It reorganizes travel scenarios and adds more useful sorting, integrated ticket booking, and itinerary planning to support both preparation and navigation around Taipei.
project_uiux_uiux1.peopleWhoRegularlyUseSmartphonesToFind: People who regularly use smartphones to find travel information
project_uiux_uiux1.peoplePlanningATripToTaipei: People planning a trip to Taipei

project_uiux_uiux1.typicalScenariosIncludeSightseeingInTaip: Typical scenarios include sightseeing in Taipei and visiting popular restaurants or distinctive attractions. Users want one place to find timely, complete, practical advice for planning and organizing a trip.
project_uiux_uiux1.earlyResearchCombinedInDepthInterviewsSu: Early research combined in-depth interviews, surveys, and competitor analysis to understand the target audience's travel behavior and identify needs unmet by existing tools.
project_uiux_uiux1.inDepthInterviewsThreeParticipantsFromOu: In-depth interviews: Three participants from outside Taipei with basic digital-tool skills shared their travel-planning experiences and thought processes.
project_uiux_uiux1.surveyWeCollected34ResponsesMainlyThroug: Survey: We collected 34 responses, mainly through the NCCU discussion board, to evaluate satisfaction factors for attractions, routes, and accommodation and to prioritize features.
project_uiux_uiux1.competitorAnalysisWeComparedKlookKkdayFu: Competitor analysis: We compared Klook, KKday, Funliday, iFoodie, and Google Maps to identify gaps in existing services.
project_uiux_uiux1.mostParticipantsReliedOnGoogleMapsFor: Most participants relied on Google Maps for planning; only a few used additional apps to book tickets or tours. Common concerns included incomplete or repetitive business information, delayed updates, inconvenient shortest-path routes, and difficulty organizing saved places.
project_uiux_uiux1.usersAlsoWantedCurrentBusinessInformatio: Users also wanted current business information, personalized sorting and filters, route and calendar integration, and access to information about accommodation cleanliness.
project_uiux_uiux1.googleMapsOfferedStrongReviewsAndRatings: Google Maps offered strong reviews and ratings but left gaps in information completeness and itinerary planning. Explore Taipei Now offered attraction categories and favorites, but had too few attractions and lacked integrated discounts and audio guides. Its itinerary tool could add stops but did not estimate travel times between them or give users a strong reason to return. Some users were also reluctant to download another travel app, highlighting the need for a clearer value proposition.
project_uiux_uiux1.theseInsightsInformedTheFollowingDesignS: These insights informed the following design strategies:
project_uiux_uiux1.integratedInformationAndInterfaceDesignR: Integrated information and interface design: Redesign attraction pages to bring together current business status and clearer navigation, reducing the effort required to search across fragmented sources.
project_uiux_uiux1.integratedTicketBookingLetUsersBookTrans: Integrated ticket booking: Let users book transport tickets within the app and access booking directly from route searches, reducing the need to switch platforms.
project_uiux_uiux1.itineraryPlanningImproveRouteOrderingAdd: Itinerary planning: Improve route ordering, add calendar synchronization, support drag-and-drop reordering, and preview transport routes. This addresses difficulties managing saved places in Google Maps and incomplete planning features in the original app.
project_uiux_uiux1.incentivesAndPopularityRankingsIntroduce: Incentives and popularity rankings: Introduce exclusive coupons and limited-time travel bundles on the homepage, alongside data-informed popularity rankings. This gives users reasons to download and revisit a platform that offers both inspiration and savings.
project_uiux_uiux1.theArchitectureCombinesFunctionalRequire: The architecture combines functional requirements with user card-sorting results to align categories with users' mental models. Five main modules are accessible through bottom navigation tabs:
project_uiux_uiux1.itinerariesRecommendedAndCustomTripsSche: Itineraries: Recommended and custom trips, scheduling, and reservations.
project_uiux_uiux1.transportPublicTransitDrivingTicketsAndC: Transport: Public transit, driving, tickets, and car rentals.

project_uiux_uiux1.onFirstUseNavigationControlsWereNot: On first use, navigation controls were not obvious. Requiring users to select GO! before starting navigation caused confusion.
project_uiux_uiux1.theBookingSuccessDialogWasEasyTo: The booking-success dialog was easy to miss, so users could overlook the entry point to their tickets.
project_uiux_uiux1.theFinalPaymentStepRequiredTooMuch: The final payment step required too much form input, slowing down booking and reducing convenience.
project_uiux_uiux1.selectingTheSearchFieldDidNotImmediately: Selecting the search field did not immediately show common categories such as restaurants or department stores, making search less efficient.
project_uiux_uiux1.theItineraryLackedDragAndDropReordering: The itinerary lacked drag-and-drop reordering, making it difficult to rearrange routes intuitively.
project_uiux_uiux1.theXRemovalIconCouldBeMistaken: The X removal icon could be mistaken for a minimize control, creating a risk of accidental deletion.
project_uiux_uiux1.attractionPagesLackedMapPositioningRevie: Attraction pages lacked map positioning, reviews were hard to find, and confirmation pages contained too much text, making itinerary management less clear.
project_uiux_uiux1.afterTheProjectIRealizedThatSeveral: After the project, I realized that several research findings had not been fully addressed in the final design. The prototype prioritized attraction search, ticket booking, and itinerary planning, revealing room to improve how I balance feature priorities and development time when handling complex requirements.
project_uiux_uiux1.problemsSuchAsOutdatedBusinessInformatio: Problems such as outdated business information and poor route suggestions often stem from database maintenance or external API limitations. They cannot be resolved through interface and visual design alone.
project_uiux_uiux1.thisExperienceShowedMeThatUiUx: This experience showed me that UI/UX designers need to understand technical boundaries as well as visual and interaction design. When underlying systems cannot change, design can still reduce effort and uncertainty through measures such as last-updated labels and user-reporting mechanisms. This is an important lesson for future redesign work.

project_uiux_uiux3.thisProjectProposesAnIntegratedOneStop: This project proposes an integrated, one-stop national examination platform to address fragmented information, complex procedures, and poor interface usability.
project_uiux_uiux3.around300000PeopleTakeNationalExaminatio: Around 300,000 people take national examinations each year. From registration and preparation to taking exams and placement, candidates must use several government websites. Fragmented information, unclear procedures, small text, and complex navigation demand considerable time and effort.
project_uiux_uiux3.surveysAndInterviewsExploredCandidatesEx: Surveys and interviews explored candidates' experiences and pain points on existing examination websites. These findings informed a one-stop platform with clear workflows and readable interfaces, helping candidates find information efficiently at every stage.
project_uiux_uiux3.candidatesCompleteTheFollowingStagesWhen: Candidates complete the following stages when taking national examinations:
project_uiux_uiux3.existingInformationChannelsSystemsAndSit: Existing information channels, systems, and site structures require candidates to navigate complicated procedures alongside studying. They must locate the appropriate site for each stage, sometimes missing information or relying on tutoring centers and previous candidates. Key problems include:
project_uiux_uiux3.fragmentedInformationDifferentAgenciesMa: Fragmented information: Different agencies manage different stages. Candidates may consult the Examination Yuan website for past papers and schedules, register on a separate site, rank placements through the Directorate-General of Personnel Administration, and request eligibility deferrals through the Civil Service Protection and Training Commission.
project_uiux_uiux3.complexInformationArchitectureExtensiveC: Complex information architecture: Extensive content makes relevant material hard to find. Examination-related tasks sit alongside other agency responsibilities, making it difficult to tailor the experience to individual candidates.
project_uiux_uiux3.unequalAccessToInformationTutoringCenter: Unequal access to information: Tutoring centers tend to compile information for popular examinations, leaving candidates for less common subjects with greater search difficulty.
project_uiux_uiux3.poorInterfaceExperienceDenseSmallTextMak: Poor interface experience: Dense, small text makes sites difficult to use and important information easy to miss, while visual presentation is unappealing.
project_uiux_uiux3.redesignServiceWorkflowsAroundPublicServ: Redesign service workflows around public-service principles.
project_uiux_uiux3.integrateExaminationResourcesIntoAOneSto: Integrate examination resources into a one-stop platform with clearer, simpler procedures.
project_uiux_uiux3.improveTheOverallUserAndServiceExperienc: Improve the overall user and service experience for candidates.
project_uiux_uiux3.thePlatformServesNationalExaminationCand: The platform serves national examination candidates—around 300,000 each year—including those preparing for exams and those managing placement preferences, eligibility deferrals, and subsequent procedures.
project_uiux_uiux3.alongsideBackgroundResearchOnExistingWeb: Alongside background research on existing websites and examination procedures, the project combines qualitative and quantitative methods to understand usability problems and information access.
project_uiux_uiux3.interviewsThreePreviousCandidatesPartici: Interviews: Three previous candidates participated, covering immigration, surveying and mapping, real estate appraisal, land administration agent, and higher-level land administration examinations. We began with their background and motivations. Participants then selected the 20 most important functions from 52 cards describing examination-site information and features. This activity also served as a probe to recall past experiences. We discussed information access and interface impressions before, during, and after examinations, and asked participants to simulate tasks to identify navigation and search difficulties.
project_uiux_uiux3.onlineSurveyDistributedThroughDcardSPubl: Online survey: Distributed through Dcard's public-service board and the NCCU discussion board, the survey collected 71 valid responses. It measured satisfaction and barriers across interface design, information access, and functionality.
project_uiux_uiux3.theQualitativeAndQuantitativeResearchIde: The qualitative and quantitative research identified four main problems:
project_uiux_uiux3.visualOverloadAndConfusingNavigationDens: Visual overload and confusing navigation: Dense, small text, complex structures, and vague navigation labels make sites hard to use and important announcements easy to miss.
project_uiux_uiux3.fragmentedChannelsInformationFromMultipl: Fragmented channels: Information from multiple agencies is spread across portals, email, and text messages. Users switch platforms frequently and often rely on Google rather than internal search.
project_uiux_uiux3.unclearProcessingStatusImportantProcedur: Unclear processing status: Important procedures, such as eligibility deferrals, still rely on paper correspondence without live online updates. Candidates must call to confirm document receipt, creating uncertainty and anxiety.
project_uiux_uiux3.timeLimitedInformationAccessAccessToOffi: Time-limited information access: Access to official information is often restricted to registration periods, making historical registration details and results difficult to retrieve for long-term preparation.
project_uiux_uiux3.visualSystemAdjustTypeSizesSpacingAnd: Visual system: Adjust type sizes, spacing, and hierarchy to reduce information overload.
project_uiux_uiux3.personalizedOneStopServicesReorganizeInf: Personalized one-stop services: Reorganize information around the stages before, during, and after examinations and integrate agency information into one platform. Store personal details and registered subjects to avoid repeated input and improve access to relevant information.
project_uiux_uiux3.liveStatusTrackingAddAProgressIndicator: Live status tracking: Add a progress indicator after document submission, with updated review status to make the process more transparent.
project_uiux_uiux3.historicalInformationAccessProvideAPerma: Historical information access: Provide a permanent archive so candidates can retrieve past examination information whenever they need it.
